elements.element: Customer is not subject to any non-compete restriction.
elements.evidence: Section 12.3 expressly states that nothing restricts Customer’s activities and that Customer has made no non-compete commitment. Section 12.4 is phrased as a permission rather than a prohibition.

elements.element: Customer is not subject to any field-of-use restriction.
elements.evidence: Section 12.3 expressly permits Customer to conduct business in any field or territory.

elements.element: Any restriction is limited to a named competing product.
elements.evidence: No operative non-compete restriction remains, so the condition requiring such a restriction to be limited to a named product is inapplicable.

elements.element: Any restriction applies only during the agreement term.
elements.evidence: No operative restriction applies during or after the term. The 24-month language in Section 12.4 qualifies an express permission, not a prohibition.

elements.element: Any restriction lasts no more than 12 months.
elements.evidence: No operative restriction exists and therefore none lasts longer than 12 months.
Sections 12.3 and 12.4 expressly permit Customer to develop products or services without excluding internal development.
Sections 12.3 and 12.4 expressly permit Customer to acquire products or services.

result.reason: The redline removes the operative non-compete by changing Section 12.4 from a prohibition to a permission, while Section 12.3 independently and unqualifiedly disclaims non-compete and field-of-use restrictions. It therefore fully satisfies the preferred position and, because no restriction remains, also satisfies each fallback limitation. The change is substantively minimal and does not disturb unrelated terms, but drafting quality is reduced by retaining a redundant, temporally limited permission that could invite unnecessary negative-implication arguments after the 24-month period; deleting Section 12.4 would be cleaner.
